title: Europe’s Hera Probe Captures First Close‑up of Battered Asteroid Dimorphos (Photo)
body:
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has captured the first direct image of Dimorphos, the 160‑metre‑wide asteroid that was deliberately struck by NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission last year. The grainy but unmistakable view shows the small moonlet’s scarred surface, confirming that the kinetic impact altered its shape and rotation. Scientists worldwide are now poring over the data, eager to gauge how the collision reshaped the binary system and to refine models of planetary‑defence strategies.

Hera, launched in October 2023 as part of ESA’s AIDA (Asteroid Impact and Deflection Assessment) partnership, entered orbit around the Didymos binary pair in early 2025 and has been conducting a series of close‑range observations. The newly released image was taken during a fly‑by at a distance of roughly 10 kilometres, using the spacecraft’s high‑resolution visible‑light camera. Although the picture is still being processed to remove motion blur and enhance contrast, the silhouette of Dimorphos is clearly discernible against the backdrop of its larger companion, Didymos. The impact crater, predicted to be a few tens of metres across, appears as a darker patch on the asteroid’s leading edge, hinting at a substantial redistribution of material.

The significance of this visual confirmation extends far beyond a single mission’s success. DART’s impact on 27 September 2022 was the first intentional attempt to alter an asteroid’s trajectory, a cornerstone test for humanity’s emerging planetary‑defence capabilities. While ground‑based telescopes measured a roughly 4‑hour reduction in Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos, the precise physical changes to the body itself remained speculative. Hera’s close‑up imagery now provides the missing piece, allowing researchers to correlate the observed orbital shift with concrete alterations in shape, mass distribution, and surface roughness.

Early analyses suggest that the impact not only excavated a crater but also displaced a significant amount of regolith, creating a cloud of debris that may have settled back onto the surface or escaped the system entirely. This redistribution could explain the measured change in the moonlet’s spin rate, which appears to have increased by a few percent according to recent radio‑science data. Moreover, the image reveals a network of fissures and boulders that were either exposed or fractured by the shock wave, offering a rare glimpse into the internal structure of a rubble‑pile asteroid. Such details are vital for refining impact‑deflection models, as they dictate how kinetic energy propagates through a loosely bound body.

The collaborative nature of the AIDA mission underscores a growing trend in space exploration: shared risk and shared reward. While NASA provided the impactor, ESA supplied the reconnaissance platform, and both agencies have pooled expertise to interpret the findings. The data from Hera will be cross‑referenced with DART’s onboard observations, ground‑based radar measurements, and computer simulations to produce a comprehensive post‑impact assessment. This holistic approach is expected to improve predictive capabilities for future deflection attempts, whether they involve kinetic impactors, gravity tractors, or even nuclear devices.

Looking ahead, Hera will continue to orbit the binary system for at least a year, mapping the surface in multiple wavelengths, measuring the mass and density of both bodies, and monitoring any long‑term changes in their orbits. The mission’s next phase includes a low‑altitude survey that could reveal hidden subsurface features and further quantify the amount of material ejected by DART. As the scientific community digests the first visual proof of Dimorphos’s altered state, the broader implication is clear: humanity now possesses both the means to test and the tools to verify asteroid deflection techniques. The success of Hera’s inaugural glimpse marks a pivotal step toward safeguarding Earth from potential future impacts, turning a once‑theoretical concept into an operational capability.
